title: Dharmendra Pradhan RESIGNS
description:
In this video we will review how the CJP protest started with the demand for Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, but gradually expanded into anti-Modi slogans, political opportunism and internal chaos. We explain how Sonam Wangchuk’s hunger strike became the movement’s biggest strength, and how the government used dialogue, ministerial outreach and promises of examination reforms to convince him to end the fast, ultimately weakening CJP’s momentum and changing the entire narrative.

We also examine how political parties, activists and controversial figures hijacked the students’ original demands, while CJP itself descended into a burger versus kachori civil war after spokesperson Vijetah Dahiya was fired. From opposition parties fighting for credit to leaders disappearing during police action, this weekly review breaks down how a genuine student movement became a political battlefield where students were eventually reduced to collateral damage.

comments.text:
I was at the protest .

What I observed was disappointing. Instead of staying focused on the real issue, some people were raising unrelated slogans and hurling abuses at our Honourable Prime Minister. I don't support any political party, but I don't believe this is the right way to address a genuine problem.

There were slogans like "Jai Bhim" and "Humko Azadi." My question is: what exactly do you mean by "Azadi" in this context? The focus should have remained on the students' legitimate concerns rather than turning the protest into a political battleground.
Disagreement with the government is completely valid—I have my own disagreements too. After all, we elect our leaders, and they are accountable to the people. But holding the government accountable is very different from resorting to personal abuse and disrespect.
I also saw a few unruly individuals throwing bottles at the police. In response, the police repeatedly used tear gas. While excessive force should always be questioned, if some protesters were provoking the police, it isn't surprising that the situation escalated. Earlier, I couldn't understand why there were reports of police action, but now I can see how such confrontations may have unfolded, even though I wasn't present at every incident.
I stand firmly with the students who are protesting peacefully for their legitimate demands. I do not stand with those who resort to violence, abuse, or actions that undermine the very cause they claim to represent.

The government's decision to seek the resignation of the concerned official was a positive step. It has helped build trust that the government is listening to the concerns of students and is willing to take action when necessary. I hope this commitment to accountability continues in the future.

At the same time, it is unfortunate to see different political parties trying to use this protest for their own political interests instead of focusing on the students' genuine concerns.

I've also come across several social media posts where people claiming to be from Pakistan and Bangladesh were expressing support for the protests. To them, I would simply say: India is fully capable of addressing its own issues. We may disagree with our government's decisions, and criticism is a normal part of a democracy, but that does not mean we seek validation or support from outside countries. We know how to raise our concerns through democratic means and resolve our issues ourselves.

My support is for peaceful, genuine student voices—not for violence, political opportunism, or attempts by anyone, inside or outside the country, to exploit a legitimate movement.
